section: A rotation curve is a speed chart
label: Paragraph
text: Plot how fast a galaxy’s stars and gas orbit against their distance from the centre. Orbit speed works like a weighing scale: the faster something orbits at a given distance, the more mass lies inside its orbit.

section: A rotation curve is a speed chart
label: List item
text: Prediction

label: Heading
text: Outer stars should slow down

label: Paragraph
text: Gravity weakens with distance. Mercury orbits the Sun at 47 km/s, Neptune at 5 km/s (Williams 2024). Most of a galaxy’s visible matter sits near its centre, so its outer stars should slow down in the same way: the dashed line.

label: List item
text: Observation

label: Heading
text: They don’t

label: Paragraph
text: By 1980 Vera Rubin and colleagues had shown that the speeds stay high, galaxy after galaxy (Rubin, Ford & Thonnard 1980). At the edge of __DEFAULT_GALAXY_NAME__, gas orbits at –, but its visible matter could only hold it at about –. Keeping it in orbit takes about – times the pull. That gap is the missing mass problem.

label: Click-to-open heading
text: How are speeds that far out measured?

label: Paragraph
text: From the Doppler shift: gas moving towards us looks slightly bluer, gas moving away slightly redder. Cold hydrogen glows faintly at 21 cm in radio, and it reaches far beyond the stars, so the speeds go further out than starlight does (Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert 2016).

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: Newton’s gravity stays as it is; there is just more mass. The simulator uses an NFW halo (Navarro, Frenk & White 1996). Its shape came out of computer simulations of dark matter clumping as the Universe grew, not from fitting rotation curves: dense in the middle, thinning outwards. Two sliders set it: mass (M200) and scale radius (rs, how spread out it is).

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: 1. Orbits. Gravity supplies the centripetal acceleration. For a round distribution of mass, only the mass M(r) inside the orbit pulls overall (Newton’s shell theorem):

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: 2. Visible matter alone. Beyond most of the stars, M(r) hardly grows, so v ∝ 1/√r: the speed should fall, like the planets’ speeds in the Solar System.

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: 3. What a flat curve needs. For v to stay constant, M(r) must grow in step with r. That happens if the density falls as 1/r²: each thin shell of thickness Δr then holds the same mass, 4πr²ρΔr, so every step outwards adds the same amount.

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: 4. The NFW density. With ρs setting how dense the halo is:

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: Well inside r<sub>s</sub> the density falls as 1/r; far outside, as 1/r³. Around r<sub>s</sub> it falls roughly as 1/r², just what step 3 needs, so over that range the halo’s speed stays nearly level. It peaks at about 2.2 r<sub>s</sub>, then falls only slowly (Navarro, Frenk & White 1996). Adding up the shells gives the mass formula used in the simulator (see Method).

section: What is a dark matter halo?
label: Paragraph
text: A known weakness. In many small, faint galaxies the inner speeds rise more gently than NFW’s dense centre allows: the cusp–core problem (de Blok 2010). Whether exploding stars could stir the dark matter enough to flatten it is still debated.

label: Heading
text: What is MOND?

label: Paragraph
text: MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) says there is no dark matter. Instead, gravity behaves differently when it is extremely weak (Milgrom 1983).

text: Schematic, not real data. Dotted line: where gravity falls to a₀. Beyond it the boost grows large and the speed levels off (Milgrom 1983).

label: Paragraph
text: MOND boosts gravity everywhere, by an amount that depends on how strong it already is. Near a galaxy’s centre gravity is strong and the boost is small; far out it is weak and the boost is large, so the outer stars keep moving fast.

label: Paragraph
text: a0 sets the scale. MOND’s constant, a0 = 1.2×10⁻¹⁰ m/s², is about 10¹¹ times weaker than gravity at Earth’s surface. It is a turning point, not a switch. With the simulator’s formula, a star speeds up by:

label: Click-to-open heading
text: Where does a<sub>0</sub> come from?

label: Paragraph
text: a0 is measured from real galaxies, not predicted. It marks the middle of MOND’s change, not where the boost starts.

label: Paragraph
text: Why ×1.6 at a0, not ×1? a0 is where MOND’s two rules cross: ×1 for strong gravity, ×√(a0 ÷ gN) for weak. Gravity rounds that corner smoothly, so the curve passes above both. The ×1.6 comes from how it is rounded, not from a0; other formulas give ×1.3 to ×1.6 (Famaey & McGaugh 2012).

label: Paragraph
text: What a0 controls. How fast the outer stars orbit: v⁴ = G M a0 (Milgrom 1983). So measured speeds pin a0 down.

label: Heading

label: Paragraph
text: Seen: galaxies in the Coma cluster move too fast for the cluster’s visible mass to hold them together (Zwicky 1933).

label: Paragraph
text: Why it matters: the first hint of missing mass. MOND shrinks the gap but still needs some unseen matter (Famaey & McGaugh 2012).

label: Heading
text: The Bullet Cluster

label: Paragraph
text: Seen: two clusters collided. Their hot gas, most of the visible matter, slowed down in the middle, but the bending of background light shows most of the mass carried on with the galaxies (Clowe et al. 2006).

label: Paragraph
text: Why it matters: the mass and the visible matter ended up in different places.

label: Text

label: Heading
text: The oldest light

label: Paragraph
text: Seen: the cosmic microwave background, light left over from the early Universe, has a pattern of slightly hotter and cooler patches.

label: Paragraph
text: Why it matters: the pattern fits a universe with about five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter (Planck Collaboration 2020).

label: Text
text: Points to MOND

label: Heading
text: Visible matter predicts the pull

label: Paragraph
text: Seen: across 153 galaxies, the pull worked out from the measured speeds closely follows one curve set only by the visible matter (McGaugh, Lelli & Schombert 2016).

label: Paragraph
text: Why it matters: MOND predicts exactly this. Dark matter can match it only if every halo is closely tied to its galaxy’s visible matter, which still needs explaining.

label: Paragraph
text: Still open

label: Heading
text: No confirmed dark matter particle

label: Paragraph
text: Decades of searches have found none (Bertone & Hooper 2018). In September 2026 the LZ experiment reported one unexplained event, but at 2.6σ it is far below the 5σ needed to claim a discovery, and it is not yet peer reviewed (LZ Collaboration 2026).

label: Heading
text: MOND beyond galaxies

label: Paragraph
text: MOND has not matched galaxy clusters or the cosmic microwave background without adding unseen matter of its own (Famaey & McGaugh 2012).

label: Heading
text: What is a mass-to-light ratio?

label: Paragraph
text: Telescopes measure a galaxy's light, not its mass. The mass-to-light ratio (M/L) converts one into the other: Suns' worth of mass per Sun's worth of light.

label: List item
text: Low M/L means young stars. Young, massive blue stars are very bright for their mass.

label: List item
text: High M/L means old stars. Old populations are mostly small, dim red stars: lots of mass, not much light.

label: Paragraph
text: SPARC’s standard values (3.6 μm infrared) are 0.5 for the disk and 0.7 for the older bulge: averages, so each galaxy differs a little. A higher M/L lifts the visible-matter curve and leaves less for dark matter.

label: Paragraph
text: Best realistic fits may scale them by 0.6 to 1.6, the range stellar models allow.

label: Paragraph
text: Source: Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert (2016), SPARC; McGaugh & Schombert (2014).

label: Screen-reader label (read aloud, not shown)
text: Close

label: Heading
text: What is the tilt?

label: Paragraph
text: We see every galaxy at an angle. The tilt (or inclination, i) is that angle: 0° is face-on, 90° is edge-on.

label: List item
text: Telescopes only see motion towards or away from us (the Doppler shift), not sideways.

label: List item
text: So a tilted disk looks slower than it really spins. True speed = measured speed ÷ sin i.

label: Paragraph
text: SPARC’s speeds are already corrected, but its tilt has an error of a few degrees. Nearly face-on galaxies are the most sensitive.

label: Paragraph
text: Best realistic fits may change the tilt within twice SPARC’s error.

label: Paragraph
text: Source: Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert (2016), SPARC; Li et al. (2018).

section: What do χ² and χ2r mean?
label: Paragraph
text: At each point, divide the gap between model and measurement by the error bar and square it; χ² is the total. χ<sup>2</sup><sub>r</sub> divides that by the number of points minus the values tuned, so galaxies and models compare fairly. Missing every point by one error bar gives about 1; by three, about 9.

label: Heading
text: Why not 0?

label: Paragraph
text: Measurements are noisy, so even a correct model misses by about one error bar.

label: Heading

label: Paragraph

label: Heading
text: Start from real measurements

label: Paragraph
text: Every speed on the Simulator comes from SPARC, a public catalogue of 175 disk galaxies (Lelli, McGaugh & Schombert 2016).

label: Paragraph
text: For each galaxy, SPARC picks a series of distances from the centre, r, and lists at each one:

label: List item
text: The measured orbit speed, Vobs, with its error bar, ±σ: the one-standard-deviation uncertainty in that speed.

label: List item
text: The speed each visible part would give on its own: the gas (Vgas), the disk of stars (Vdisk) and the central bulge (Vbulge). SPARC works these out from radio maps of the hydrogen gas and infrared (3.6 μm) images of the starlight from the Spitzer Space Telescope.

label: Paragraph
text: The site reads SPARC’s table as published for __GALAXY_NAMES__; no speed is typed in or adjusted. (The Custom Sandbox galaxy is imaginary, so it has none.)

label: Heading
text: Correcting for tilt

label: Paragraph
text: A telescope only sees motion towards or away from us (the Doppler shift), so a tilted disk looks slower than it really spins. SPARC divides by sin i, where the tilt i is 0° face-on and 90° edge-on:

label: Click-to-open heading
text: What if SPARC’s tilt is slightly off?

label: Paragraph
text: SPARC’s tilt, i<sub>SPARC</sub>, has an error of a few degrees. If the true tilt is i, every speed changes by the same factor (Li et al. 2018, eq. 5):

label: Paragraph
text: Example: SPARC says 60° but the truth is 55°: s = 0.866 / 0.819 ≈ 1.06, so the real speeds are 6% higher. At 30° instead of 25°, s ≈ 1.18. Nearly face-on galaxies are far more sensitive.

label: Paragraph
text: With Best realistic fits on, each model may change i by up to __FIT_LIMIT_SIGMA__× SPARC’s error (never past 90°). The page leaves the points where SPARC put them and divides the model by s instead, which gives the same score.

label: Heading
text: Add up the visible matter

label: Paragraph
text: How fast things would orbit if only the visible stars and gas pulled: the cyan dashed line.

label: Paragraph
text: Why add squares? For a circular orbit, the pull is g = V²/r, so V² = gr. The pulls of the gas, disk and bulge add up, so their V² values add too. The square root at the end turns the total back into a speed.

label: Paragraph
text: Turning starlight into mass. Telescopes measure starlight, not mass. The two numbers in the formula are mass-to-light ratios: Suns’ worth of mass per Sun’s worth of infrared light. SPARC’s standard 0.50 (disk) and 0.70 (older bulge) come from models of how ageing stars change in light and mass (McGaugh & Schombert 2014). In use now: standard SPARC values.

label: Paragraph
text: V<sub>bar</sub> is the speed a star would have if only the visible matter pulled on it.

label: Click-to-open heading
text: Why multiply by the mass-to-light ratio?

label: Paragraph
text: SPARC gives V<sub>disk</sub> and V<sub>bulge</sub> for a ratio of 1. V² is proportional to mass, so doubling the ratio doubles the stars’ mass and doubles their V².

label: Click-to-open heading
text: Why V<sub>gas</sub>|V<sub>gas</sub>| instead of V<sub>gas</sub>²?

label: Paragraph
text: Much of a galaxy’s gas lies in a ring further out. Inside a flat ring, the near side pulls harder than the far side, so near the centre the gas pulls outwards overall and SPARC lists V<sub>gas</sub> as negative. (Newton’s shell theorem, that only the mass inside you pulls, holds for a round cloud but not for a flat disk.) V<sub>gas</sub>|V<sub>gas</sub>| keeps the minus sign that squaring would lose, so there the gas lowers the total.

label: Paragraph
text: In the Custom Sandbox you set the masses yourself, so nothing needs converting from light. The stars and the gas are flat disks that fade steadily outwards (exponential disks), and the bulge is a ball of stars (a Hernquist profile).

label: Paragraph
text: Their speeds add as squares, for the same reason as in a real galaxy: V² = gr, and pulls add.

label: Paragraph
text: The thin dotted lines on the rotation curve show each part on its own.

label: Heading
text: Supply the missing pull

label: Paragraph
text: The measured speeds sit above the cyan line, so something must pull harder. Each idea gives a different answer: the orange line.

The model adds no dark matter beyond it.

label: Heading
text: Score the fit

label: Paragraph
text: How far each orange line misses the measured points, with their error bars as the ruler.

label: Paragraph
text: For each point, find the gap between the model and the measurement, divide it by that point’s error bar and square it. Add these up to get χ² (“chi-squared”). Squaring means misses above and below both count, and big misses count far more than small ones.

label: Paragraph
text: Then divide by N − k, the number of points minus the number of values tuned to fit this galaxy. The result, χ2r, is roughly the squared miss per point. About 1 means the curve misses by about one error bar: as close as the measurements allow.

label: Paragraph
text: Why subtract k? A model with more dials can always be bent closer to the data, so each dial counts against it. With standard values, k = 0 for visible matter only and for MOND at the measured a0 (1 if you set a0 yourself), and 2 for the halo (its mass and scale radius, even when set by hand). Best realistic fits tune more: k = __K_NFW_FIT__ for the halo and __K_MOND_FIT__ for MOND.

label: Paragraph

section: Watch stars move under that gravity
label: Paragraph
text: Test stars feel the model’s gravity but do not pull on each other. There are 800 for NGC 3198, scaled with visible mass (200 to 2400): a display choice, since a real galaxy has billions.

section: Watch stars move under that gravity
label: Paragraph
text: They start in balance. Disk stars start on circular orbits at the measured speeds; bulge stars get random motions (a velocity dispersion) that hold the bulge up, much as pressure holds up a gas. With too little pull they drift outwards, and past 1.5 × the visible edge they count as ejected.

section: Watch stars move under that gravity
label: Paragraph
text: The pull on each star gives it an acceleration a = Vmodel(r)²/r towards the centre.

label: Heading
text: One small step at a time

section: One small step at a time
label: Paragraph
text: An orbit cannot be solved in one go, so the computer moves each star in small steps of Δt = 0.5 Myr, 2000 times over 1 Gyr (the velocity-Verlet method). First the position, as in SUVAT’s s = ut + ½at²:

section: One small step at a time
label: Paragraph
text: Then it finds the acceleration at the new position, a<sub>new</sub>, and updates the velocity with the average of the old and new accelerations:

section: One small step at a time
label: Click-to-open heading
text: Why this method?

section: One small step at a time
label: Paragraph
text: Using only the old acceleration (Euler’s method) makes each step slightly wrong in a way that builds up, so the orbit’s energy drifts and stars slowly spiral in or out. Velocity-Verlet is symplectic: its energy error stays small and bounded instead of growing, so a star that leaves does so because of the physics, not the size of the step.

label: Heading
text: What this model leaves out

label: Paragraph
text: The simplifications that matter most, so you can judge the results yourself.

label: List item
text: A round pullThe 3D view treats the galaxy’s mass as a ball, though the disk is flat. The rotation curve uses SPARC’s own disk calculations and is unaffected; the stars’ bobbing is approximate.

label: List item
text: A softened centreNear the centre the pull is smoothed over 0.5 to 1 kpc and is exactly Newtonian beyond 2.8 softening lengths (the GADGET-2 spline; Springel 2005), so close passes don’t fling stars out.

label: List item
text: A smooth, round haloThe halo is perfectly smooth and stops at r200. In many small, faint galaxies, the speeds near the centre suggest a flatter middle than NFW’s (the cusp–core problem; de Blok 2010).

label: List item
text: Estimated star massesMass-to-light ratios are averages, not measured per galaxy. Best realistic fits vary them within limits.

label: List item
text: Hard limitsBest fits stop sharply at each range’s edge. With softer limits, Li et al. (2018) found acceptable MOND fits for most SPARC galaxies.

label: List item
text: Four galaxiesSPARC has 175. Four show the method; they cannot decide between the ideas.

label: List item
text: Drawn, not calculatedThe glow, star spikes, purple halo cloud and MOND’s gold shading are visual aids. They change no numbers.

label: List item
text: Spiral arms are drawn onThe test stars don’t pull on each other, so they can’t form arms. The drawn arms follow density-wave theory (Lin & Shu 1964): a slower pattern the stars pass through, lit mostly by young stars and absent in gas-poor disks. Their shape and speed are a visual choice.
